title: Athanasius against the world
hook: exiled again and again, he held to Nicaea when it was unpopular

segments.voice: Yesterday, homoousios, and your line was true god from true god. What everyday word did you catch doing a lot of work? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Winning the vote isn't the end of an argument. Nicaea chose its word, and then the argument kept going. Bishops who'd signed changed their minds. Emperors came and went, and some of them leaned toward Arius' side. And one stubborn bishop of Alexandria, named Athanasius, would not let the word go. He was sent away from his city, and came back, and was sent away again, and came back again. He hid. He wrote. He was accused of crimes, and answered the charges in writing. Later generations gave him a short Latin nickname: Athanasius contra mundum. Athanasius against the world. It didn't look like a hero on a hill. It looked like a man packing a bag, again.

What was he holding on to? In his book On the Incarnation, Athanasius gives the reason Nicaea mattered to him, in one swing of a sentence. In paraphrase: God became human, so that humans might become divine. Only God can bring people home to God, he argued. If the Son is a creature, however grand, the bridge doesn't reach. So for him homoousios wasn't a word game. It was the whole rescue. Now the exiles. He's sent as far as Trier, in Gaul, a long way from the Nile. Other times he simply disappears into Egypt, and he's sheltered, the stories say, by the desert monks. That's a thread from a few days ago: Athanasius later wrote the Life of Antony, the man who heard a Gospel line read in church, and went into the desert. Here's a surprise. When enemies mocked him for running instead of staying to die, he wrote a defense of his flight. Jesus himself withdrew when they sought to kill him, he pointed out. And Paul, in his own words, escaped Damascus this way: "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." Standing firm, for Athanasius, didn't mean standing still for the soldiers. It meant not changing the word. Run if you must, hide if you must, but don't sign what you believe is false. Was he easy to deal with? His opponents certainly didn't think so, and they brought real charges against him, which he denied. He could be a hard man to cross. But the nickname stuck because, for long stretches, he seemed to be nearly alone, and he didn't move.
screen: `GOD BECAME HUMAN, SO HUMANS MIGHT RISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you hold to be true that, in some room you're in, isn't popular. At work, at a family table, with friends. It doesn't need to be about faith. Let it come. Then test it, slowly. Is this a truth, or is it my pride wearing a truth's clothes? If it holds up, what's one way to hold it that isn't cruel to the people who disagree? Athanasius ran, hid and wrote. He didn't have to win every room. If you pray, you can bring this to God. If not, just sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Athanasius against the world. A later nickname for the bishop of Alexandria who, exiled again and again, kept holding to the word of Nicaea when it was unpopular.
Your line: against the world. Today, if the truth you named comes up, say it once, plainly and kindly, and then let it stand. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and other churches honor Athanasius as a saint and teacher of the faith, and his On the Incarnation is still read in churches and classrooms.
